title: Prime Factorization
description: Break a number into its prime building blocks, quickly and for many queries

blocks.text: Prime factorization means writing a number as a product of primes, like 60 equals 2 times 2 times 3 times 5. Because primes are the building blocks of every integer, this decomposition unlocks a whole family of problems.
Once you have the prime factors, you can quickly count divisors, compute GCDs, and reason about a number structure.

Every integer greater than 1 can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way, apart from the order. This is the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, and it is why prime factorization is so powerful.

blocks.caption: A factor tree for 60, breaking it down to 2 times 2 times 3 times 5

blocks.text: We usually write repeated primes with exponents, so 60 becomes 2 squared times 3 times 5. Those exponents carry a lot of information about the number.

The simplest way is to try dividing by each candidate starting from 2. While the current candidate divides n, pull it out and record it, then move on. Any remaining value above 1 at the end is itself a prime factor.
Just like primality testing, we only need to try divisors up to the square root of n, which keeps it fast.
Here is the square root based trial division.

codes.python:
def factorize(n):
    factors = []
    i = 2
    while i * i <= n:
        while n % i == 0:          # pull out i as many times as it divides
            factors.append(i)
            n //= i
        i += 1
    if n > 1:
        factors.append(n)          # leftover prime
    return factors

blocks.text: This runs in O(sqrt n) for a single number, which is fine for one off queries.
If you must factorize many numbers up to some limit, the square root method per query is too slow. Instead, run a modified sieve that stores, for each number, its smallest prime factor.

blocks.caption: Precompute the smallest prime factor of every number, then divide it out repeatedly

blocks.text: With that table, factorizing any number is just repeatedly dividing by its smallest prime factor. Each step removes at least one prime, so it takes only about log n divisions.

Trade off:

The smallest prime factor sieve costs O(n) memory and one preprocessing pass, but then every factorization is nearly instant. Use it when you have many queries in a fixed range.
Once you can factorize, several other results come almost for free.

items: The number of divisors, from the exponents of the prime factors
The sum of divisors, using a formula on those exponents
The GCD and LCM, by comparing the primes of two numbers
Checking if a number is a perfect square or a prime power

blocks.text: Prime factorization is the bridge from a raw number to its deep structure, which is why it shows up across so many maths problems.
